titre: A Fish Known Only as a Fossil Came Up in a Trawler
accroche: On December 22, 1938, a museum curator finds, in the catch of a South African trawler, a fish thought extinct for 66 million years.
contenu_vulgarise:
On December 22, 1938, at the South African port of East London, Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer receives a call from Captain Hendrik Goosen. She is a curator at the local museum and has asked him, like the other trawler captains, to let her know if an unusual marine animal turns up in the nets. On the deck of the Nerine, she finds a fish a meter and a half long, pale blue mottled with light spots, with thick scales and fleshy fins at the end of a muscular lobe, a bit like stumps of a limb. None of her reference books shows anything like it.

## An Animal Science Ranked Among the Fossils

Courtenay-Latimer preserves the fish as best she can, having it mounted for lack of a way to freeze it, and sends a description to James Leonard Brierley Smith, an ichthyologist at Rhodes University. The mail takes weeks to reach him. When Smith finally sees the mounted specimen, on February 16, 1939, he immediately recognizes a coelacanth, a group of fleshy-finned fishes that geologists had known until then only from fossils. The most recent of these fossils dates from about 66 million years ago, the end of the Cretaceous, the time of the disappearance of the non-avian dinosaurs. Science therefore held coelacanths to be extinct since that date, like an entire branch that had stopped short.

## Naming a Genus After Its Discoverer

Smith publishes his description in March 1939 in the journal Nature and names the species Latimeria chalumnae: the genus in honor of Courtenay-Latimer, the species after the Chalumna River, near which the Nerine was fishing. It then takes Smith fourteen years to find a second specimen, in 1952, this time in the Comoros, where local fishermen had long known the animal under the name gombessa and occasionally caught it without seeing anything extraordinary in it.

## What a Fossil That Still Breathes Changes

The discovery does not make the coelacanth lineage any younger: it merely shows that part of this lineage kept on existing without leaving an identified fossil trace for 66 million years, in deep waters off the Comoros and then, later, in Indonesia, where a second, distinct species was described in 1999. Nothing in the anatomy of Latimeria earned the species the nickname “living fossil” that the press pinned on it: the term mostly says how thoroughly the absence of a recent fossil had convinced naturalists that the entire group had vanished. An incomplete fossil record never proves an extinction, it only proves that nothing has yet been found after a certain date, and it took a South African trawler to recall the difference.

repere.texte: The last known coelacanth fossil dated from about 66 million years ago. It took until December 22, 1938 for a living specimen to come up in the nets of a South African trawler, and fourteen more years for a second to be found, in 1952, in the Comoros.

carte.punch: This fish was known only as a fossil. It came up alive from a trawler in 1938.
carte.idee: On December 22, 1938, a South African museum curator finds in a trawler's catch a fleshy-finned fish unknown to her reference books. It is a coelacanth, a group that paleontology held to be extinct for 66 million years, for lack of a more recent fossil.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Presentation of the biology of the living coelacanth and of the discovery of a second species in Indonesia in 1999.

quiz.question: Why did the discovery of the living coelacanth in 1938 make such a mark on naturalists of the time?
choix: Because it was the largest fish ever caught off South Africa
Because it was the first marine species discovered thanks to an industrial trawler
Because this group of fishes was known only from fossils, and was thought extinct for 66 million years
Because the fish had lungs able to breathe air
quiz.explication: Neither the fish's size nor an ability to breathe air explains the event: what struck naturalists was that an animal considered extinct since the end of the Cretaceous, for lack of a more recent fossil, turned out to be very much alive. Industrial trawlers had long been bringing up unknown marine species, so this was not a first.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer manage to preserve the fish, lacking a way to freeze it?
choix: She puts it in formalin at the museum
She sends it back alive to the sea with a tag
She makes only a detailed drawing of it, without keeping the specimen
She has it mounted by a taxidermist
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Unable to freeze the fish, Courtenay-Latimer has it mounted as best she can before sending her description to the ichthyologist James Leonard Brierley Smith, who will not see the specimen until February 16, 1939.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the scientific name Latimeria chalumnae come from?
choix: From Courtenay-Latimer's name for the genus, and from the Chalumna River for the species
From the name of the trawler Nerine and its captain Hendrik Goosen
From the name of Smith, who described the species, and of Rhodes University
From the local name gombessa given by Comorian fishermen
quiz_supplementaire.explication: James Leonard Brierley Smith names the genus Latimeria in honor of Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, who brought the fish to his attention, and the species chalumnae after the Chalumna River, near which the Nerine was fishing.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the discovery of a second specimen in the Comoros in 1952 reveal?
choix: That the species had only just appeared in that region
That it was a species distinct from the one discovered in 1938
That local fishermen had long known the animal, without finding it extraordinary
That the coelacanth had developed new anatomical abilities since 1938
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It takes Smith fourteen years to find a second specimen, in 1952, in the Comoros, where local fishermen had long known the animal under the name gombessa and caught it without seeing anything extraordinary in it.
